summary: Defines a standard set of field names for online shopping forms, so wallet software can fill in payment and address details automatically. This first version of the Electronic Commerce Modeling Language is informational. It was replaced by RFC 3106.

eli5.summary: When shops all name their form boxes the same way, a helper can fill your name and address everywhere quickly, like a pen that knows each form.

subtitle: Standard names for form fields so wallets can fill them in automatically.

tldr.problem: Online shoppers have to manually fill in name, address, and payment information at many different merchant websites, each with different field names. About two-thirds of shopping forms are abandoned during this tedious process.
tldr.mechanism: ECML Version 1 defines a standard set of HTML form field names for billing address, shipping address, payment card details, and other commerce data. When merchants use these field names, digital wallet software from multiple vendors can automatically fill them in, reducing the burden on customers.
tldr.outcome: Merchants can adopt ECML by making simple changes to their HTML forms, and customers benefit from faster checkout with wallets that support the standard. ECML was replaced by RFC 3106.

today: RFC 2706 is an Informational RFC from October 1999, developed by a vendor consortium outside of the IETF. It was replaced by RFC 3106, which updated the ECML specification.

sections.title: The Problem and the Standard
sections.content:
Before ECML, every e-commerce merchant designed their own HTML forms with their own field names. Customers were confused by the variety, and many gave up rather than finish the checkout. Digital wallets—software that stores billing, shipping, payment and preference information—could help, but they were hampered by the lack of standard field names.

ECML Version 1 solves this by documenting a simple, consistent set of field names that merchants can use. The fields cover shipping address, billing address, receipt address, payment card details, order IDs, and metadata like schema version and transaction completion flags. Version 1 targets North American consumer-to-merchant commerce and avoids more complex features like business cards or non-card payment methods, which were deferred to future versions.
sections.eli5: Instead of each shop making up its own form, they all agree to use the same names. Your wallet app then knows what to fill in everywhere.

sections.title: Field Organization and Naming
sections.content:
ECML field names are hierarchically organized using underscores. For example, Ecom_ShipTo_Postal_City for the shipping city and Ecom_BillTo_Postal_City for the billing city. This hierarchy allows systems to request and transmit aggregates: a wallet might provide all address fields under Ecom_ShipTo, and the merchant's system unpacks them according to the transmission protocol.

The standard covers fields like name (with optional prefix and suffix), street addresses (up to three lines), postal code, country code, phone, and email. Billing, shipping, and receipt fields mirror each other in structure. Card details include name, type (VISA, MASTERCARD, etc.), number, expiration date components, and verification value. All field names must be used exactly as specified; only the visual labels shown to users can vary.
sections.eli5: The form boxes have names like "Ecom_ShipTo_City" and "Ecom_BillTo_City". The underscore separates the parts. A wallet reads these names and knows what to fill.

sections.title: Activating Wallets and Multi-Page Transactions
sections.content:
A wallet application is triggered when it detects ECML fields or the user takes action. The Ecom_SchemaVersion field (usually hidden) identifies the version of ECML being used and should appear on every page; it is recommended as the last ECML field so a wallet knows when the page has finished loading.

Merchants can ask for information across multiple web pages. The Ecom_TransactionComplete field (usually hidden) signals the final page of a transaction, allowing wallets to stop filling fields and protecting customer privacy by not continuing to auto-fill for unrelated pages. Merchant software remains flexible: it can require all fields to be provided or make them optional, and may re-request information if needed or if validation fails.
sections.eli5: The wallet watches for a special hidden box called Ecom_SchemaVersion. When it finds it at the end of a page, it knows the form is ready. Another box, Ecom_TransactionComplete, tells it when your shopping is done.

sections.title: Compatibility and Implementation
sections.content:
ECML is not a replacement for SSL/TLS, SET, XML, or IOTP—these standards handle encryption, non-repudiation, and other important functions that ECML does not. ECML can be used with any payment mechanism. Version 1 adds no new technology; merchants can adopt it by making simple changes to their existing HTML forms, and use of ECML requires no license.

Multiple wallets and merchants planned to support ECML interoperably, making it an open standard. The specification targets North American consumer commerce, and the RFC itself notes that the data model is heavily biased toward United States conventions and the English language, making it less suitable for international or multilingual use. All field sizes specified are minimum data entry sizes, not maximum or exact values.
sections.eli5: ECML works alongside other security and payment systems. It is just a list of names. Merchants don't need permission to use it, and any wallet software can learn to fill ECML fields.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The information requested by ECML fields—credit card numbers, addresses, phone numbers—is sensitive and should be protected when sent over the internet. ECML does not specify protection mechanisms, but channel encryption such as SSL/TLS or IPSec would be appropriate. Users must be able to control which of their information is released to protect privacy.

Wallet software that fills forms across multiple pages should check for the Ecom_TransactionComplete field and cease automated filling when it is encountered, pending further authorization, to avoid revealing customer information to unrelated merchants.
sections.eli5: The card and address information is private and should be encrypted when sent over the internet. The wallet should stop auto-filling when the transaction ends so you don't accidentally share info with another shop.
